::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## What you will do

Grow one decision tree and watch it overfit; then grow five hundred and average them. You will fit a random forest
through the same workflow as this morning's logistic regression, estimate its performance honestly with
cross-validation, read its out-of-bag error, and ask it which variables it leans on.

**Time:** 30 min live coding + 25 min *Your turn*.
:::

## 0 · Start where Tutorial 1 ended

```{r}
#| label: setup
# WHERE WE ARE ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tutorial 1 built the whole pipeline: -9 -> NA, codes -> factors, drop the leaky biomarkers, stratified split,
# 5 folds, the recipe (impute -> dummy -> zero-variance -> normalise), a workflow, and the logistic baseline.

source("R/prep_nhms.R")   # nhms, dm_data, dm_split, dm_train, dm_test, dm_folds, dm_rec, cls_metrics
library(rpart.plot)

```

## 1 · One decision tree

::: {.callout-note}
## In one paragraph
A classification tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions. At each node it tries every predictor and every
cut-point, and keeps the split that makes the two child nodes **purest** — lowest **Gini impurity**
$1 - \sum_k p_k^2$ (0 = all one class, 0.5 = a coin toss). It repeats inside each child until a stopping rule
fires. A leaf's prediction is the proportion of *Yes* among the training people who landed there. Continuous
predictors are split at *thresholds* (BMI ≥ 27.5), which is why trees find cut-offs that nobody told them about
— and why a tree's prediction surface is a staircase, never a slope.
:::

Trees do not need dummy variables or scaling, so a leaner recipe keeps the splits readable:

```{r}
#| label: tree-rec
tree_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())
```

### A small, pruned tree

```{r}
#| label: tree-small
#| fig-height: 6
tree_small <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0.005, tree_depth = 4, min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_small_fit <- workflow(tree_rec, tree_small) |> fit(dm_train)
tree_small_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE, extra = 104, type = 2)
```

Read it like a clinical algorithm: the root split is the single most informative question; each leaf shows the
probability of *Yes* and the share of people who end up there.

| Lever | `decision_tree()` argument | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| minimum people in a node before it may split | `min_n` | larger → simpler |
| maximum depth | `tree_depth` | smaller → simpler |
| cost-complexity pruning: a split must improve impurity by at least α | `cost_complexity` | larger → fewer leaves (CART's `cp`) |

### An unconstrained tree — the overfitting signature

```{r}
#| label: tree-big
tree_big <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, tree_depth = 30, min_n = 2) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")
tree_big_fit <- workflow(tree_rec, tree_big) |> fit(dm_train)

bind_rows(
  small_train = augment(tree_small_fit, dm_train) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  small_test  = augment(tree_small_fit, dm_test)  |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  big_train   = augment(tree_big_fit,   dm_train) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  big_test    = augment(tree_big_fit,   dm_test)  |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes),
  .id = "model"
)
```

The big tree is near-perfect on the data it was grown on and *worse than the small tree* on new data. It memorised
noise: somewhere in it is a leaf that says "age < 23.5 and waist > 101 → Yes" because one person happened to fit.
Everything that follows in this workshop is a way of growing trees without memorising.

::: {.callout-warning}
We peeked at `dm_test` to make the overfitting point vivid. That is the last time until Tutorial 5. From here on,
honest estimates come from the five folds of the **training** set.
:::

## 2 · Random forest: many noisy trees, averaged

::: {.callout-note}
## In one paragraph
**Bagging**: draw a bootstrap sample of the training rows, grow a full unpruned tree, repeat 500 times, and
predict by voting. Each tree is a noisy, high-variance estimate; averaging many of them cancels the noise without
adding bias — *provided the trees differ*. The **random forest** twist makes sure they do: at every split, a tree
may only consider a random subset of `mtry` predictors, so the trees do not all put `age` at the root and become
near-copies of each other. The rows left out of each bootstrap sample (about a third) are **out-of-bag** and give
every tree a free validation set; the forest's **OOB error** is an honest estimate you get without cross-validation.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-spec
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 6, min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation", seed = 2026) |>
  set_mode("classification")

rf_wf <- workflow(tree_rec, rf_spec)
```

| Knob | Meaning | Heuristic | Bias–variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mtry` | predictors tried at each split | √p for classification (here ~5–6) | higher → trees more alike; lower bias, more correlation |
| `trees` | number of trees | 500–1000; more never hurts, only costs time | more → lower variance, until it plateaus |
| `min_n` | smallest node that may be split | 5–10; larger smooths the probabilities | higher → simpler trees, more bias, less variance |

### Honest estimate: 5-fold cross-validation on the training set

```{r}
#| label: rf-cv
set.seed(2026)
rf_res <- fit_resamples(rf_wf, resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics,
                        control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))
collect_metrics(rf_res)
```

Mean and standard error across five folds. The standard error is the number most papers forget to report — and
the one that tells you whether two models actually differ.

### Fit once on all the training data, and look inside

```{r}
#| label: rf-fit
rf_fit <- fit(rf_wf, dm_train)
rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine()      # note "OOB prediction error (Brier s.)" - a free validation estimate
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-importance
rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> ranger::importance() |>     # the permutation importances ranger computed on the OOB rows
  tibble::enframe(name = "variable", value = "importance") |>   # tibble is not attached by tidymodels any more, hence the ::
  slice_max(importance, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(importance, reorder(variable, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0b4f6c") +
  labs(x = "permutation importance (rise in OOB error when the column is shuffled)", y = NULL,
       title = "Random forest: permutation importance") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Importance tells you **which** variables the forest leans on, not **how** (direction, shape, thresholds). Two
caveats: impurity-based importance is biased toward continuous and many-level predictors (we used permutation
importance, which is fairer); and **correlated predictors share credit** — `bmi`, `waist`, `weight` and `bmi_cat`
each look less important than "adiposity" really is. Tutorial 6 adds partial dependence and SHAP for the *how*.

### Compared with this morning's baseline

```{r}
#| label: rf-vs-lr
lr_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm"))
set.seed(2026)
lr_res <- fit_resamples(lr_wf, dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics)

bind_rows(logistic = collect_metrics(lr_res), random_forest = collect_metrics(rf_res), .id = "model") |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "pr_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean, y = model, colour = model)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = mean - std_err, xmax = mean + std_err), show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ .metric, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "5-fold CV estimate (± 1 SE)", y = NULL, title = "Same folds, same recipe idea, two model families")
```

Look at the error bars before declaring a winner. On tabular survey data a well-built logistic regression is hard
to beat; the forest earns its extra AUC where the truth has interactions and thresholds (and here it does — the
simulator planted several).

## Your turn (25 min)

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Task A · The five-minute forest
Four hand-picked forests, compared on the **folds** (never on the test set). Fill the three TUNE lines with your
own guesses, run, and see who in the room finds the best setting. Think about accuracy *and* computation.

```{r}
#| label: taskA
#| eval: false
forests <- list(
  heuristic = rand_forest(mtry = 6,   trees = 500,  min_n = 10) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  model_1   = rand_forest(mtry = ___, trees = ___,  min_n = ___) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),   # TUNE
  model_2   = rand_forest(mtry = ___, trees = ___,  min_n = ___) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),   # TUNE
  model_3   = rand_forest(mtry = ___, trees = ___,  min_n = ___) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification")    # TUNE
)

set.seed(2026)
forest_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(tree = tree_rec), models = forests) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026, verbose = TRUE)

rank_results(forest_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

**A1.** Did any of your settings beat the heuristic by more than one standard error?
**A2.** Which took longest (watch the `verbose` output)? Was the time worth it?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution A

```{r}
#| label: solA
forests <- list(
  heuristic = rand_forest(mtry = 6,  trees = 500,  min_n = 10) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  wide      = rand_forest(mtry = 15, trees = 500,  min_n = 10) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  deep      = rand_forest(mtry = 6,  trees = 500,  min_n = 2)  |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  smooth    = rand_forest(mtry = 4,  trees = 1000, min_n = 40) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification")
)
set.seed(2026)
forest_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(tree = tree_rec), models = forests) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)

rank_results(forest_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

Typically everything lands within ~0.01 AUC and within one standard error. Random forests are famously forgiving
— which is their great virtue and why tomorrow's tuning session concentrates on XGBoost instead. Larger `min_n`
usually improves the **Brier** score (smoother, better-calibrated probabilities) even when AUC is flat. Doubling
`trees` roughly doubles the time and buys almost nothing beyond 500 here.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Task B · Does the forest see the same world as the GLM? (10 min)
Compare the top-10 permutation importances from `rf_fit` with the top-10 odds ratios (by |z|) from the logistic
model in Tutorial 1. Where do they agree? Where do they differ, and can you explain the difference from how the
two models work?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution B

```{r}
#| label: solB
lr_fit <- fit(lr_wf, dm_train)
tidy(lr_fit) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> arrange(desc(abs(statistic))) |> select(term, estimate, statistic) |> head(10)
rf_fit |> extract_fit_engine() |> ranger::importance() |> tibble::enframe("variable", "importance") |> arrange(desc(importance)) |> head(10)
```

Both put age, family history, BMI/waist and ethnicity at the top. Differences: the GLM spreads `ethnic` over four
dummy coefficients while the forest scores the factor once; the forest gives `waist` and `bmi` *both* high
importance (it uses either interchangeably), the GLM concentrates the effect on one of them and leaves the other
small; and interaction-only effects (family history × obesity) show up in the forest's importances but cannot
appear in a GLM without an interaction term.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Task C · Stretch
1. The OOB Brier score printed by `ranger` vs the 5-fold CV Brier from `collect_metrics(rf_res)`: how close are
   they? Why would you still cross-validate?
2. Refit `rf_spec` with `set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity")`, pull `ranger::importance()` again and
   compare the ranking to the permutation version. Which variables move, and why? (Hint: think about how many
   distinct values each has.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution C
1. They are usually within a few thousandths. OOB is free and honest *for the forest itself*, but it cannot
   evaluate the **pre-processing** (imputation, dummies) because those were estimated on all training rows, and it
   cannot compare the forest with models that have no OOB concept. Cross-validation evaluates the whole workflow.
2. Impurity importance inflates continuous variables with many split points (`hh_income`, `waist`, `age`) and
   deflates binary ones (`fam_hx_dm`, `sex`), because a variable with more candidate cut-points has more chances
   to reduce impurity by luck. Permutation importance does not have this bias — prefer it.
:::

## What to remember

1. A single tree is a readable clinical algorithm that overfits unless pruned.
2. Random forest = bagging + random feature subsets; nearly tune-free; OOB error for free.
3. Report mean ± SE from resamples, not one number.
4. Importance says *which*, not *how*. The *how* is Tutorial 6.

**Next:** Tutorial 3 — support vector machines (Session 4, 15.50).
